_meta.description: Trimmed from an original 21-paper/50-question set down to 9 foundational papers, after live EVAL-001 ingestion showed the combined free-tier LLM budget (Gemini + Groq + OpenRouter) supports ~1-2 fully-ingested papers/day — 21 papers would have taken 2-3 weeks. These 9 still span encoder-only/decoder-only/encoder-decoder architectures and the core NLP pretraining-objective debates, which is what the question set actually needs. Single-hop questions are answerable from one paper's own text (vanilla RAG should do fine). Multi-hop questions require combining facts across 2+ papers via shared entities/lineage — deliberately the largest category here, since that's the actual thing EVAL-002 is trying to prove GraphRAG wins at. Comparison questions ask for an explicit contrast between two papers' claims or design choices.
_meta.note: Papers must be downloaded and ingested manually (POLISH-004 ArXiv auto-import isn't built yet) via the Papers page upload — arxiv_id below is the download source, not an auto-import mechanism.

papers.title: Attention Is All You Need
papers.role: Introduces the Transformer architecture (self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding) that every other paper in this set builds on.

papers.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
papers.role: Encoder-only, masked language modeling + next sentence prediction (NSP).

papers.title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners (GPT-2)
papers.role: Decoder-only, autoregressive language modeling, zero-shot task transfer.

papers.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)
papers.role: Decoder-only, scaled to 175B parameters, in-context few-shot learning without gradient updates.

papers.title: RoBERTa: A Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach
papers.role: Re-tunes BERT's pretraining recipe: removes NSP, dynamic masking, larger batches/more data.

papers.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (T5)
papers.role: Encoder-decoder, casts every NLP task as text-to-text.

papers.title: ELECTRA: Pre-training Text Encoders as Discriminators Rather Than Generators
papers.role: Encoder-only, replaced-token-detection objective (generator+discriminator) instead of MLM.

papers.title: XLNet: Generalized Autoregressive Pretraining for Language Understanding
papers.role: Permutation language modeling with two-stream self-attention — autoregressive but bidirectional-context, avoids BERT's [MASK] pretrain/finetune mismatch.

papers.title: DistilBERT, a distilled version of BERT: smaller, faster, cheaper and lighter
papers.role: Knowledge-distills BERT into a 6-layer student (~40% smaller, ~60% faster, ~97% of BERT's performance).

questions.question: What two components make up the encoder-decoder Transformer introduced in 'Attention Is All You Need', and what mechanism replaces recurrence/convolution entirely?
questions.gold_answer: An encoder stack and a decoder stack, each built from multi-head self-attention and position-wise feed-forward layers; self-attention (with positional encodings added to the input embeddings, since attention has no inherent sense of order) replaces recurrence and convolution entirely.

questions.question: What are BERT's two pretraining objectives?
questions.gold_answer: Masked language modeling (MLM) — predict randomly masked tokens from bidirectional context — and next sentence prediction (NSP) — predict whether one sentence follows another.

questions.question: How does GPT-2 perform downstream tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning?
questions.gold_answer: Zero-shot: GPT-2 is a single autoregressive language model conditioned only on the input text (and natural-language task framing/prompt), with no architecture changes or gradient updates for the specific task.

questions.question: How large is the largest GPT-3 model, and how does it perform new tasks at inference time?
questions.gold_answer: 175 billion parameters. It performs new tasks via in-context, few-shot (or zero/one-shot) learning: task examples are given as text in the prompt, with no gradient updates or fine-tuning.

questions.question: Name three specific changes RoBERTa makes to BERT's pretraining recipe.
questions.gold_answer: Any three of: removes the next sentence prediction (NSP) objective, uses dynamic masking (masking pattern generated each time a sequence is fed to the model, not fixed once at preprocessing), trains with much larger batch sizes, trains on significantly more data for longer, and uses a larger byte-level BPE vocabulary.

questions.question: What is T5's central idea for handling many different NLP tasks with one model?
questions.gold_answer: Cast every text-based NLP task (translation, classification, summarization, regression scored as text, etc.) into the same text-to-text format, so one encoder-decoder Transformer with one training objective and decoding procedure can be used for all of them, differentiated only by a task-specific text prefix.

questions.question: What pretraining objective does ELECTRA use instead of masked language modeling, and what two networks does it involve?
questions.gold_answer: Replaced token detection: a small generator network replaces some tokens with plausible alternatives, and a discriminator network is trained to predict, for every token, whether it was replaced by the generator or is original.

questions.question: What is XLNet's core pretraining objective, and what BERT limitation is it designed to avoid?
questions.gold_answer: Permutation language modeling — an autoregressive objective that maximizes the expected log-likelihood over all possible orderings (permutations) of the factorization order, giving it bidirectional context. It avoids BERT's pretrain-finetune discrepancy caused by relying on the artificial [MASK] token during pretraining, which never appears during fine-tuning/inference.

questions.question: How is DistilBERT trained, and what performance/size tradeoff does the paper report?
questions.gold_answer: Via knowledge distillation from a BERT teacher during pretraining, using a triple loss (distillation loss, masked language modeling loss, and a cosine-embedding loss). It reports roughly 40% fewer parameters and about 60% faster inference than BERT, while retaining about 97% of BERT's language-understanding performance.

questions.question: XLNet and ELECTRA both aim to fix a weakness in how BERT uses the [MASK] token during pretraining. What is that weakness, and how does each paper's fix differ?
questions.gold_answer: The weakness: BERT pretrains with an artificial [MASK] token that never appears during fine-tuning/inference, creating a pretrain-finetune mismatch, and BERT also assumes masked-out tokens are predicted independently of each other. XLNet's fix is to never use [MASK] at all — it uses permutation language modeling, an autoregressive objective over random factorization orders, so every token is predicted from real tokens only. ELECTRA's fix is different: instead of masking, a small generator model substitutes plausible replacement tokens for some positions, and the main model (a discriminator) is trained to detect which tokens were replaced — real tokens appear in every input, corrupted only by substitution, not masking.

questions.question: RoBERTa and DistilBERT both start from BERT but pursue opposite goals. Contrast what each optimizes for and the core technique each uses to get there.
questions.gold_answer: RoBERTa optimizes for maximum accuracy by more thoroughly pretraining the same BERT-style masked-language-model architecture: no architecture change, but more data, larger batches, longer training, dynamic masking, and no NSP. DistilBERT optimizes for the opposite — a much smaller, faster model that keeps most of BERT's accuracy — via knowledge distillation, training a 6-layer student model to match a full BERT teacher's output distribution (plus its own MLM and embedding-similarity losses), roughly halving depth while retaining ~97% of performance.

questions.question: GPT-2 and GPT-3 are both decoder-only autoregressive language models from the same research lineage. What is the key methodological shift between them in how they're evaluated/used on downstream tasks?
questions.gold_answer: GPT-2 is evaluated purely zero-shot: it performs tasks from a natural-language prompt alone, with no task examples shown and no parameter updates. GPT-3 introduces in-context few-shot (and one-shot/zero-shot) learning as its central evaluated setting: a handful of input-output examples for the task are placed directly in the prompt alongside the query, letting the frozen model condition on demonstrations without any gradient-based fine-tuning — GPT-3's paper explicitly studies how performance scales with the number of in-context examples and with model size.

questions.question: Every model in this set derives from the Transformer in 'Attention Is All You Need', but they don't all keep both the encoder and decoder. Group BERT, GPT-2, and T5 by architecture (encoder-only / decoder-only / encoder-decoder) and explain the general task-type implication of each choice.
questions.gold_answer: BERT is encoder-only, well suited to understanding tasks (classification, tagging, extractive QA) since it produces bidirectional contextual representations but has no built-in generation mechanism. GPT-2 is decoder-only, well suited to open-ended text generation since it's autoregressive by construction (predicts each token from only the tokens before it). T5 keeps both the encoder and decoder, making it naturally suited to sequence-to-sequence tasks (translation, summarization) as well as understanding tasks recast as text generation, since it can both encode bidirectional input context and autoregressively generate output.

questions.question: ELECTRA and DistilBERT both claim to improve on BERT's efficiency, but at different points in a model's lifecycle. Contrast where each saves cost.
questions.gold_answer: ELECTRA saves cost during pretraining — its replaced-token-detection objective gets a learning signal from every token in every example (not just a masked ~15%), so it reaches a given quality level with less pretraining compute, but the resulting discriminator model is the same size/speed as a comparable BERT at inference time. DistilBERT saves cost at inference/deployment time — it produces a genuinely smaller, shallower model (via knowledge distillation from a BERT teacher) that runs faster and has fewer parameters, at the cost of a separate distillation stage on top of an already-pretrained teacher, not a cheaper pretraining objective itself.

questions.question: GPT-2 and T5 both frame downstream tasks partly through text itself rather than a task-specific output head, but they differ in whether the model's weights change per task. Explain the difference.
questions.gold_answer: GPT-2 uses natural-language task framing at inference time only — the same frozen, zero-shot-evaluated model's weights never change per task; the 'instruction' is just part of the prompt text. T5 uses a text prefix too, but T5 is fine-tuned (its weights ARE updated via gradient descent) on labeled data for each task; the prefix mainly tells one already-adapted model which task it was fine-tuned for, since T5's paper's primary results come from per-task fine-tuning, not zero-shot prompting.

questions.question: RoBERTa and XLNet were both published as direct responses to BERT within roughly the same year, but they pull on different levers. Contrast what each paper changes.
questions.gold_answer: RoBERTa changes the training *recipe* while keeping BERT's masked-language-model objective and architecture exactly as-is: more data, longer training, larger batches, dynamic masking, no NSP. XLNet changes the pretraining *objective* itself, replacing masked language modeling with permutation language modeling (plus a two-stream self-attention mechanism to make that objective work) — a genuinely different architecture/objective, not just a better-tuned version of BERT's own approach.

questions.question: XLNet's two-stream self-attention is a modification of the self-attention mechanism from 'Attention Is All You Need'. Why does XLNet need two streams instead of the original single attention stream?
questions.gold_answer: The original Transformer's self-attention lets each position attend to token content at every position, which works for BERT/encoder-style bidirectional prediction but would let XLNet's permutation-based prediction of a token 'see' its own content — trivializing the prediction. XLNet's two-stream mechanism splits this into a content stream (carries full token content, like ordinary self-attention) and a query stream (can access position information and earlier tokens' content, but not the current target token's own content), letting it predict each token autoregressively over a random permutation order without ever leaking the answer to itself.

questions.question: BERT and T5 both use a masking/corruption-based pretraining signal, but T5 changes what the model has to predict. Contrast BERT's masked language modeling with T5's span-corruption objective.
questions.gold_answer: BERT's MLM masks individual random tokens and predicts each one directly in place, within an encoder-only architecture that outputs one prediction per masked position. T5's primary pretraining objective corrupts contiguous spans of tokens (replacing each dropped span with a single sentinel token) and trains the encoder-decoder model to generate just the missing spans as output text — a generative, sequence-to-sequence reconstruction task rather than a per-position classification task, consistent with T5's whole text-to-text framing.

questions.question: GPT-3 and DistilBERT represent opposite scaling strategies that both claim to solve a practical problem. What problem does each address, and in which direction does each scale?
questions.gold_answer: GPT-3 scales up (to 175B dense parameters) to address task generality/flexibility — a single frozen model that can perform many tasks from prompting alone, without task-specific fine-tuned models. DistilBERT scales down (to a 6-layer, ~66M-parameter student via distillation) to address deployment cost — making a BERT-quality model cheap enough to run at inference time in resource-constrained settings, at the cost of being fine-tuned per task like BERT rather than prompted.

questions.question: T5 and XLNet both make an argument about the *right* pretraining objective, but they argue for it differently. Contrast T5's approach to justifying its design choices with XLNet's.
questions.gold_answer: T5's paper justifies its choices empirically and broadly — it runs a large systematic ablation study comparing many architectures, objectives, and datasets within one unified framework, and picks the best-performing combination found. XLNet's paper instead argues analytically for one specific alternative objective (permutation language modeling) as fixing named theoretical weaknesses in BERT's MLM (the independence assumption and the pretrain-finetune [MASK] mismatch), supporting it with a narrower, targeted set of comparisons against BERT rather than a broad architecture/objective sweep.

questions.question: ELECTRA and RoBERTa both push back on how BERT was pretrained, but they diagnose a different root problem. What does each paper implicitly argue was wrong with BERT's original pretraining?
questions.gold_answer: RoBERTa implicitly argues BERT's architecture and objective were fine, but BERT was simply undertrained relative to its capacity — the fix is more/better training (data, batch size, duration, dynamic masking), not a new objective. ELECTRA implicitly argues the MLM objective itself is inefficient regardless of training budget, since it only produces a learning signal from a masked subset of tokens per example — the fix is replacing MLM with replaced-token-detection, which uses every token as a training signal.

questions.question: BERT and GPT-2 are contemporaries built on the same Transformer building blocks. Contrast their core architectural choice and what it implies for the tasks each is naturally good at.
questions.gold_answer: BERT keeps only the Transformer's encoder and trains with masked language modeling, giving it bidirectional context — strong for understanding/classification tasks but no native way to generate text left-to-right. GPT-2 keeps only the decoder and trains autoregressively (predict the next token from only prior tokens), giving it strictly left-to-right context — strong for open-ended text generation but weaker at tasks that benefit from seeing full bidirectional context at once.

questions.question: ELECTRA's paper argues its replaced-token-detection objective is more sample-efficient than BERT's masked language modeling. What is the core reason given?
questions.gold_answer: MLM only produces a learning signal from the (typically ~15%) masked-out tokens in each example, ignoring the rest. ELECTRA's discriminator must classify every single token in the input as original or replaced, so the model gets a training signal from all tokens in every example, not just a masked subset — making more efficient use of the same amount of data/compute.

questions.question: GPT-3's few-shot in-context learning and T5's text-to-text transfer are both framed as general solutions to 'one model, many tasks.' How do the two approaches fundamentally differ in how a new task is specified to the model?
questions.gold_answer: GPT-3 specifies a new task entirely through the prompt at inference time — a natural-language instruction and/or a handful of input-output demonstration examples placed in the context window — with no parameter updates at all. T5 specifies a new task by fine-tuning (updating the model's actual weights) on labeled data for that task, using a short text prefix in the input mainly to tell one already-adapted model which of several tasks it was fine-tuned/is being used for, not to teach it a brand-new task purely from the prompt.

questions.question: XLNet's paper positions permutation language modeling as strictly better than BERT's masked language modeling. What specific BERT assumption does XLNet's paper single out as a weakness that permutation LM avoids?
questions.gold_answer: BERT's paper (via its MLM objective) assumes the masked tokens in a sequence are predicted independently of each other given the unmasked context, ignoring dependencies between the masked tokens themselves. XLNet's permutation LM predicts each token conditioned on all previously-seen tokens in the sampled permutation order (which can include other 'masked' positions once they've been generated earlier in that permutation), so it doesn't make that independence assumption.

questions.question: ELECTRA and DistilBERT are both framed as 'efficient' alternatives to standard BERT-style pretraining, but contrast which stage of a model's lifecycle each actually improves.
questions.gold_answer: ELECTRA improves pretraining-time efficiency — reaching strong downstream results with less pretraining compute, since every token (not just a masked subset) contributes a training signal via its discriminator objective. DistilBERT doesn't make pretraining itself more efficient (it requires a fully-pretrained BERT teacher first); it improves inference-time efficiency, producing a smaller, faster model to deploy via a separate distillation stage after pretraining is already done.

questions.question: RoBERTa and XLNet both improved on BERT's benchmark results, but reviewers of the two papers would ask a different follow-up question about generality. What would that difference be?
questions.gold_answer: Because RoBERTa changes only the training recipe (data/duration/batching/masking) and not the objective or architecture, its gains are easy to attribute directly to "BERT was undertrained" and are straightforward to replicate on other MLM-style models. Because XLNet changes the pretraining objective and architecture (permutation LM, two-stream attention) together with also using more data than BERT, its reported gains are harder to cleanly attribute to the new objective alone versus the additional data/compute used alongside it — a natural follow-up question the paper itself partly acknowledges by including ablations.
